relevance_reason: The paper reports a healthy adult who is homozygous for an HAO1 frameshift knockout and has isolated glycolic aciduria and elevated plasma glycolate. This patient directly characterises the GYCA phenotype.

findings.statement: McGregor et al. (2020) described a healthy British-Pakistani woman in her fifth decade who carried a lifelong complete HAO1 knockout. She was identified by exome sequencing of autozygous population cohorts (Born in Bradford and Genes and Health). She was overweight (BMI 30-35 kg/m2) and the mother of 3 healthy children. A renal ultrasound was normal, and apart from common short-term illnesses she was otherwise healthy. The authors concluded that lifelong HAO1 knockout was safe and without clinical phenotype in this woman.
quotes: At the time of assessment, she was in her 5th decade and a mother with three healthy children. She declared British-Pakistani ethnicity. Renal ultrasound, carried out as part of a gynaecology assessment, was normal.
She was overweight (BMI 30–35 kg/m2), and other than common non-serious short-term illnesses and pregnancy symptoms, otherwise healthy.
In this woman, lifelong HAO1 knockout is safe and without clinical phenotype, de-risking a therapeutic approach and informing therapeutic mechanisms.

findings.statement: In the HAO1-null woman, McGregor et al. (2020) found plasma glycolate of 171 nmol/mL (reference 14 or less), about 12 times the upper limit of normal. Her urinary glycolate/creatinine ratio was 199 to 309 mg/g (reference 50 or less), about 6 times the upper limit of normal. Plasma and urinary oxalate, plasma glycerate, the serum anion gap and standard serum biochemistries were all normal.
quotes: At genotype directed recall, her serum anion gap was normal, and plasma and urinary oxalate were both normal.
her plasma glycolate and urinary glycolate levels were markedly elevated (Table 1), at, respectively, 12 times and six times the upper limit of normal in healthy reference individuals.
Plasma glycolate | 171 nmol/mL | ≤14

findings.statement: McGregor et al. (2020) profiled 1,871 plasma metabolites and lipids in the woman and compared them with 25 controls. Of these, 18 biochemicals, including glycolate, were markedly elevated (more than 5 SD above controls). Unconjugated bile acids were elevated and glycine- and taurine-conjugated bile acids were reduced, which the authors suggested might reflect reduced local availability of glycine. Six of the elevated metabolites had structures compatible with being potential HAO1 substrates.
quotes: We observed that 18 biochemicals (including glycolate) were markedly elevated (extreme outliers at >5 sd compared to controls) in addition to other more modestly elevated biochemicals (Supplementary file 1 and 2).

The elevated cholic acid related compounds might be due to reduced local availability of glycine (a product of the glycolate pathway) to conjugate cholic acid and its bile acid derivatives (unconjugated bile acids are elevated; glycine and taurine conjugated bile acids are reduced).
Six of the significantly elevated metabolites have a structure compatible with being potential HAO1 substrates

findings.statement: In the woman, McGregor et al. (2020) identified a homozygous 1-bp deletion in the HAO1 gene (c.997delC, rs1186715161), predicted to cause a frameshift (Leu333SerfsTer4) that truncates the final 37 amino acids. The variant was found by exome sequencing of blood DNA and confirmed by Sanger sequencing of saliva DNA. It lay within a 5.2-Mb autozygous region, and she was not homozygous for any other rare predicted loss-of-function variant. No homozygous predicted loss-of-function HAO1 variants were present in gnomAD v2.1.
quotes: The frameshift variant, rs1186715161 (present on a single Ensembl 99 transcript ENST00000378789.3:c.997delC, ENSP00000368066.3:p.Leu333SerfsTer4), for which the woman is homozygous, is predicted to truncate the final 37 amino acids of the HAO1 protein.

The volunteer was 7.4% autozygous at the DNA level and the genotype was within a long (5.2 Mb) autozygous region. She was not homozygous for any other rare (minor allele frequency <1%) predicted loss-of-function genotypes.
No complete knockout (homozygous predicted loss of function, pLOF) variants in HAO1 were observed in the online gnomAD v2.1 database of 141,456 whole exome/genome sequenced individuals

findings.statement: McGregor et al. (2020) expressed the p.Leu333SerfsTer4 HAO1 variant in CHO-K1 cells. The variant protein was markedly reduced and diffusely mislocalised, whereas mRNA levels were unaffected. The authors linked this to loss of the C-terminal SKI peroxisomal targeting tripeptide. Using lumasiran phase 1 data from healthy volunteers for comparison, they estimated that the woman retained less than 2% residual glycolate oxidase activity.
quotes: Results with p.Leu333SerfsTer4 revealed markedly reduced HAO1 protein (mRNA levels were unaffected) with the p.Leu333SerfsTer4 HAO1 protein also diffusely distributed (mis-localised) within cells.
HAO1 protein is normally found exclusively in hepatocyte peroxisomes and requires the C-terminal tripeptide SKI for this targeting (Recalcati et al., 2001).
Consequently, we estimate that this woman likely retains <2% residual glycolate oxidase activity.

findings.statement: McGregor et al. (2020) reported that about 1 in 2,700 individuals in gnomAD v2.1 is heterozygous for an HAO1 predicted loss-of-function variant. They estimated that the expected frequency of homozygotes in an outbred population is about 1 in 30 million.
quotes: The cumulative frequency of known pLOF variants in HAO1 is low, in gnomAD v2.1 approximately 1 in 2700 individuals is heterozygous.
since the expected homozygote frequency in an outbred population would be only ~1 in 30 million individuals

findings.statement: McGregor et al. (2020) concluded that the clinically silent lifelong HAO1 knockout supports the potential safety of chronic HAO1 inhibition, such as with the RNAi therapeutic lumasiran, for treating primary hyperoxaluria type 1.
quotes: Most importantly, our data support the potential safety of HAO1 inhibition as a chronic therapy for the devastating metabolic disease PH1.

relevance_reason: Reports the first patient with isolated glycolic aciduria and a homozygous HAO1 splice-site mutation, which establishes the genetic basis of this disorder.

findings.statement: Frishberg et al. (2014) reported 2 brothers, born to consanguineous healthy parents of Arab descent, who were evaluated for psychomotor delay associated with a triple-A-like syndrome (anisocoria, alacrima, and achalasia). The proband had markedly increased urinary glycolic acid excretion, with normal excretion of oxalate, citrate, and glycerate. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with normal echotexture. The authors found that the genetic cause of the triple-A-like syndrome in this family was unrelated to the metabolic abnormality, and they described the glycolic aciduria as isolated and asymptomatic.
quotes: Two brothers, born to consanguineous healthy parents of Arab descent, were evaluated for psychomotor delay associated with triple-A-like syndrome (anisocoria, alacrima and achalasia).

The proband showed markedly increased urinary glycolic acid excretion with normal excretion of oxalate, citrate and glycerate. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with normal echotexture.
The genetic nature of triple-A-like syndrome in this kindred was found to be unrelated to this metabolic abnormality.

phenotypes.text: markedly increased urinary glycolic acid excretion

findings.statement: In a patient of Arab descent with isolated glycolic aciduria, born to consanguineous parents, Frishberg et al. (2014) used direct sequencing of the HAO1 gene and identified a homozygous splice-site mutation (c.814-1G>C) at the invariant -1 position of the intron 5 splice acceptor site. HAO1 is expressed specifically in the liver, so the authors tested the mutation with an in vitro hybrid-minigene assay. Cells transfected with the mutant minigene produced an abnormal splice variant. The authors concluded that expression of a defective glycolate oxidase splice variant causes isolated asymptomatic glycolic aciduria.
quotes: Direct DNA sequencing of glycolate oxidase gene (HAO1) revealed a homozygous c.814-1G>C mutation in the invariant -1 position of intron 5 splice acceptor site.

Since HAO1 is a liver-specific enzyme, the effect of this novel mutation on splicing was validated by an in vitro hybrid-minigene approach. We confirmed the appearance of an abnormal splice variant in cells transfected with mutant minigene vector.
Our results pinpoint the expression of defective splice variant of glycolate oxidase as the cause of isolated asymptomatic glycolic aciduria.

findings.statement: Frishberg et al. (2014) suggested that the observation that loss of glycolate oxidase causes only asymptomatic glycolic aciduria supports developing substrate reduction as a new treatment approach for primary hyperoxaluria type I.
quotes: This observation contributes to the development of novel approaches, namely, substrate reduction, for the treatment of primary hyperoxaluria type I.
